preview_text: เข่าที่ร้อนและบวมซึ่งรู้สึกดีขึ้นเมื่ออยู่ด้วยน้ำแข็ง และความหนาวเย็นที่ปวดเข่าซึ่งต้องการความอบอุ่น เป็นสองสภาวะที่แตกต่างกันโดยสิ้นเชิงใน TCM โดยแต่ละสภาวะมีวิธีการรักษาของตัวเอง และแต่ละ...
categories: ["เงื่อนไขข้อและข้ออักเสบ"]
synonyms: ["Bi syndrome of the knee", "Crane’s Knee Wind"]
conventional_description: In Western medicine, Knee Bi Syndrome most closely aligns with knee osteoarthritis (OA) - a degenerative joint disease where the protective cartilage cushioning the ends of bones wears down over time. Symptoms include pain, stiffness, swelling, and a grating sensation with movement. Diagnosis is typically made through a combination of physical examination, X-rays showing joint space narrowing and bone spurs, and sometimes MRI. Risk factors include age, obesity, previous joint injury, and genetic predisposition.
conventional_treatments: Standard Western treatments aim to manage symptoms and maintain function. They include over-the-counter pain relievers (acetaminophen, NSAIDs like ibuprofen), prescription anti-inflammatory medications, physical therapy to strengthen supporting muscles, corticosteroid or hyaluronic acid injections into the joint, and in advanced cases, total knee replacement surgery. Lifestyle modifications such as weight loss and low-impact exercise are also recommended.
tcm_understanding:
TCM understands Knee Bi Syndrome through the lens of obstruction, or 'Bi' (痹). The knee is a meeting point for several major channels, and when the flow of Qi and blood through these channels is blocked - whether by external pathogens like Dampness, Cold, or Heat, or by internal weakness - pain and stiffness follow. The Liver governs the sinews and the Kidneys govern the bones, so when these organ systems are depleted over time, the joint loses its structural support and becomes vulnerable to obstruction.
External factors are also key. Living in a damp environment, exposure to cold and wet weather, or even a diet that creates internal Dampness can allow pathogenic factors to settle in the knee. Dampness is heavy and sticky; it sinks downward and combines easily with Heat or Cold, producing hot, swollen joints or cold, aching ones.
Blood Stagnation, often from an old injury or chronic obstruction, creates a fixed, stabbing pain that worsens at night.
Because the root cause can be excess (Damp Heat, Blood Stasis) or deficiency (Liver and Kidney weakness, Kidney Yang deficiency), the same Western diagnosis of knee osteoarthritis can have multiple TCM patterns. A knee that feels hot and swollen with a greasy yellow tongue coating points to Damp Heat obstruction.
A knee that aches deeply, feels cold, and is accompanied by fatigue and frequent nighttime urination points to Kidney Yang deficiency. Each pattern has its own treatment logic.
classical_quote: 「风寒湿三气杂至，合而为痹也。... 以冬遇此者为骨痹，以春遇此者为筋痹... 痹在于骨则重，在于脉则血凝而不流，在于筋则屈不伸...」
classical_translation: "When the three qi of wind, cold, and dampness arrive together and intermingle, they form a Bi syndrome. ... Encountering these in winter causes bone Bi; in spring, sinew Bi. ... When Bi is in the bone, there is heaviness; in the vessels, blood congeals and does not flow; in the sinews, there is bending without extension."
classical_source:
Huang Di Nei Jing Su Wen  ,  Chapter 43: Discussion on Bi Syndrome (痹论) 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
Painful Obstruction due to Damp Heat in Channels presents with a knee that feels hot, swollen, and red. The pain worsens with pressure and improves with cold compresses. You may also feel generally warm, thirsty, and have a greasy yellow coating on your tongue. The pulse feels rapid and slippery. This pattern often arises after prolonged exposure to damp, hot environments or internal heat accumulation.
Blood Stagnation pattern is marked by sharp, stabbing pain that is fixed in one location and often intensifies at night. The knee may not look hot or swollen, but the pain is deep and piercing. The tongue appears dark purple or has small purple spots, and the pulse feels wiry or choppy. This pattern often develops from chronic obstruction or injury that has not resolved, leading to poor blood flow in the knee.
Painful Obstruction with Liver and Kidney Deficiency produces a dull, chronic ache with a sense of weakness and stiffness, especially after activity. The knee may feel better with rest and gentle warmth. This pattern is common in older adults or those with long-standing wear and tear. The tongue is pale and thin with a thin white coating, and the pulse is thin and weak. It reflects an underlying lack of nourishment to the sinews and bones.
Kidney Yang Deficiency pattern adds a distinct deep coldness to the knee, along with overall cold intolerance, low back soreness, and fatigue. The knee may feel icy to the touch, and the pain is worse in cold weather. The tongue is pale and swollen with a white coating, and the pulse is deep, slow, and weak. This pattern indicates the body’s warming fire has declined, and it often appears in advanced or long-standing cases.

patterns.pattern_name: Painful Obstruction due to Damp Heat in Channels
patterns.symptoms: ["Knee feels hot and looks red", "Swelling around the knee that is hot to the touch", "Pain worsens with warmth or pressure", "Pain improves with cold applications", "Heavy, aching sensation in the leg", "Thirst with desire to drink", "Irritability and restlessness"]
patterns.worse_with: Hot weather or humid environment, Spicy and greasy foods, Alcohol, Overexertion or prolonged standing, Warm compresses or heat
patterns.better_with: Cold applications, Rest, Cooling foods (e.g., cucumber, watermelon), Gentle movement
patterns.why_this_happens: When dampness and heat combine and settle into the knee joint, they block the normal flow of Qi and blood. This creates a hot, swollen, and intensely painful knee that feels worse with warmth or pressure. The body tries to fight the heat with thirst and restlessness, while the dampness makes the leg feel heavy and stiff.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly slightly swollen, with a yellow greasy coating. Pulse: slippery and rapid, may be soggy or wiry at the Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-heat is a combination of pathogenic dampness and heat. Heat aggravates the heat component, so warmth, hot weather, and spicy foods worsen the redness and pain, while cold applications and cooling foods soothe it. Dampness is heavy and sticky, so humidity and prolonged standing increase swelling and heaviness, whereas rest and gentle movement help drain dampness and prevent stagnation.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol, which create more damp-heat. Eat cooling, damp-draining foods like mung beans, barley, cucumber, and watermelon. Rest the knee and apply cool packs, but keep gentle movement to prevent stiffness. Avoid hot baths or saunas.

patterns.worse_with: Cold, damp weather, Prolonged inactivity, Pressure on the knee, Stress

patterns.why_this_happens: When Qi and blood flow become obstructed in the knee joint, perhaps from an old injury or chronic wear, blood stasis forms. This stagnant blood cannot nourish the sinews and bones, leading to a fixed, stabbing pain. The pain worsens at night because stillness allows the stasis to settle, and pressure further blocks the already sluggish flow.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with stasis spots and distended dark sublingual veins. Pulse: choppy (涩 sè) or wiry (弦 xián).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and damp constrict the blood vessels, making stasis worse, while inactivity allows blood to pool. Pressure directly aggravates the blocked flow. Stress stagnates Liver Qi, which further impedes blood circulation. Gentle movement and warmth promote the smooth flow of Qi and blood, and massage helps break up local stasis.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the knee warm and avoid prolonged sitting or standing. Gentle, regular movement like walking or tai chi helps circulate blood. Eat warming, blood-moving foods like turmeric, ginger, and small amounts of red meat; avoid cold, raw foods and excessive dairy that congeal blood.

patterns.pattern_name: Painful Obstruction with Liver and Kidney Deficiency
patterns.symptoms: ["Chronic dull ache in the knees", "Lower back soreness and weakness", "Worse in cold or damp weather", "Fatigue and lack of stamina", "Stiffness and limited movement", "Pale or dull complexion"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold, damp weather, Overexertion or prolonged standing, Cold or raw foods and drinks
patterns.better_with: Warm compresses or heat applications, Gentle movement, Warm, cooked foods, Rest
patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver nourishes the sinews and the Kidneys govern the bones. When Liver blood and Kidney essence are depleted over time, the knees lose their structural support and natural lubrication. This leaves the joint vulnerable to wear and tear, producing a chronic, dull ache and a sense of weakness that worsens in cold or damp weather because the body lacks the internal warmth to circulate Qi and blood efficiently.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale and thin with a thin white coating. Pulse: fine, weak, and slow, especially weak in the Chi (rear) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and damp weather further deplete the body's deficient yang Qi and constrict the channels, making the already malnourished knees feel worse. Warmth and nourishing foods support the Liver and Kidney, while gentle movement promotes circulation without draining the limited reserves of Qi and blood.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the knees warm with wraps or long clothing, especially in damp or cold weather. Eat warm, cooked foods like bone broths, stews, and root vegetables; avoid raw, cold, and iced items. Gentle daily movement such as Tai Chi or walking on flat ground keeps Qi flowing without exhausting the joints.

patterns.worse_with: Cold, damp weather, Overexertion or prolonged standing, Cold or raw foods and drinks, Fatigue and lack of sleep, Sitting in a draft
patterns.better_with: Warm compresses or heat applications, Rest, Gentle movement, Warm, cooked foods, Moxibustion
patterns.why_this_happens: The Kidneys are the root of the body's warming Yang energy. When Kidney Yang is deficient, the internal fire cannot warm the joints, allowing cold and damp to settle in the knees. This leads to deep, aching cold pain, stiffness, and weakness, as the bones and sinews lack the warmth needed to stay strong and supple. The deficiency also causes systemic symptoms like fatigue, frequent urination, and cold intolerance.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, tender body with teeth marks and a wet white coating. Pulse: deep, slow, and weak, especially at the Chi (Kidney) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yang is the body's fundamental fire; cold and damp directly deplete it, while warmth supports it. Overexertion and fatigue drain Yang further, so rest conserves it. Warm foods and moxibustion supply Yang to the knees, easing cold pain. Gentle movement keeps Qi and blood flowing without exhausting the Kidneys.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the knees warm with wraps or knee pads, especially in cold or damp weather. Eat warm, cooked foods like stews and soups, and use warming spices such as ginger, cinnamon, and cloves. Avoid cold drinks and raw foods. Gentle exercise like tai chi or walking helps maintain joint mobility without draining Yang. Moxibustion at home on the lower abdomen or lower back can be very beneficial.

faqs.question: What exactly is Knee Bi Syndrome?
faqs.answer: Knee Bi Syndrome is the TCM diagnosis that most closely corresponds to knee osteoarthritis. It refers to a condition where pain, stiffness, and swelling arise from obstruction of Qi and blood in the knee channels. The obstruction can be caused by external pathogens like Dampness and Heat, or by internal weakness of the Liver, Kidney, and Spleen systems. Unlike Western medicine, TCM distinguishes several patterns within this syndrome, each with a different treatment.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help chronic knee pain?
faqs.answer: Yes, many studies and centuries of clinical experience support acupuncture for knee osteoarthritis. Acupuncture works by unblocking the channels around the knee, reducing inflammation, and promoting local blood flow. Points like Yanglingquan (GB-34) and Zusanli (ST-36) are often combined with points that address the underlying pattern - for example, Taixi (KI-3) to nourish the Kidneys in deficiency cases. Most patients feel some relief after the first few sessions, though lasting change requires a course of treatment.

faqs.question: How long before I notice improvement?
faqs.answer: Many people feel a reduction in pain and stiffness after 2-4 weeks of consistent treatment. Excess patterns, like Damp Heat, often respond faster because the focus is on clearing pathogens. Deficiency patterns, where the body’s reserves need to be rebuilt, take longer - typically 3-6 months. Your practitioner will adjust the treatment plan as you progress, and may recommend maintenance sessions to prevent recurrence.

faqs.question: Can I keep taking my pain medication while doing TCM?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can be safely combined with most conventional pain medications. Herbs and acupuncture may reduce your need for painkillers over time, but never stop prescribed medications abruptly. Always inform both your TCM practitioner and your medical doctor about everything you’re taking. Blood-moving herbs like Dan Shen or Hong Hua may interact with anticoagulants (warfarin, aspirin), so full disclosure is essential.

faqs.question: Do I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a supportive role. In general, avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that promote Dampness - think ice cream, salads, fried foods, and dairy. Instead, favor warm, cooked meals like soups and stews. Anti-inflammatory spices such as turmeric and ginger can be helpful. Your practitioner may give more specific advice based on your pattern, such as avoiding spicy foods in Damp Heat or eating more warming foods in Kidney Yang deficiency.

faqs.question: Will the acupuncture hurt?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture needles are hair-thin and insertion feels more like a quick pinch or a dull ache - not a sharp pain. Around the knee, you may feel a sensation of heaviness or distension as the Qi arrives, which is a normal sign of a good treatment. Most patients find sessions relaxing and often fall asleep.

research.title: Effectiveness of acupuncture as adjunctive therapy in osteoarthritis of the knee: a randomized, controlled trial
research.description: This landmark RCT assigned 570 patients with knee osteoarthritis to either true acupuncture, sham acupuncture, or an education control group. After 26 weeks, patients receiving true acupuncture had significantly greater improvements in pain and function compared to sham and control groups, establishing acupuncture as a viable adjunctive treatment.
research.periodical: Berman BM, Lao L, Langenberg P, et al. Ann Intern Med. 2004;141(12):901-910.

research.title: Acupuncture for osteoarthritis of the knee
research.description: This Cochrane systematic review analyzed 16 RCTs involving 3498 participants. The authors concluded that acupuncture provides short-term, clinically relevant improvements in pain and physical function for knee osteoarthritis compared to sham acupuncture or no intervention, with a low risk of serious adverse effects.
research.periodical: Manheimer E, Cheng K, Linde K, et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2010;(1):CD001351.

research.title: Acupuncture for osteoarthritis of the knee: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This meta-analysis of 12 RCTs found that acupuncture significantly reduced pain intensity and improved functional mobility compared to sham controls. The study highlighted that the benefits of acupuncture were superior to standard care and comparable to NSAIDs but with fewer side effects.
research.periodical: Cao L, Zhang XL, Gao YS, et al. Acupunct Med. 2012;30(3):187-193.
